Ecologists might have heard this frequently. I have always wondered what that means." categories: - Multivariate Analysis filters: - openlinksinnewpage - nutshell execute: echo: true citation: true format: html: comments: giscus: repo: zzzhehao/giscus category: Announcements mapping: url reactions-enabled: true theme: light: light_tritanopia dark: dark_dimmed --- ::: {.cell} ::: In my bachelor's, we learned statistics in the traditional way - we learned different tests, test for variances, test for correlations, t-test, u-test, chi-square test, ANOVA, blahblah. We didn't really touch the core of statistics, we also didn't know where those tests come from, they were like natural theorems in statistics - they simply exist. So does multivariate statistics. When I did my first DCA (detrended correspondence analysis), I had no idea what multivariate analysis was, because I didn't even realize all the statistics I had been playing with were univariate. That was two years ago. I got an assignment, a script, and it opened the door to the whole world of numerical ecology for me. After that, I learned PCA, PCoA, NMDS, t-SNE, blahblah, but same as the tests, we are only taught when to use them, what they produce, but not why to use them, why not to use them, and what they exactly do. The Black Box principle can be useful, but not this time. The more one uses a certain tool, the more important it is for them to understand the tool. And apparently, ordination is at the heart of answering many ecological questions. ![The course report I wrote with my first DCA: "Gradient Analysis of the Floodplain Grassland: Species Community"](assets/DCA_report.png){width="60%"} Since then, I realized that I see the word "ordination" quite often in different literature, but I never really understood it, I can't draw links between the word with anything else in my daily life, nor with any real-life ecology. They are like a floating city in the ocean of knowledge. It kept growing, but never had an anchor point. Once I read the word again in the help document of the function `cmdscale()` from the base R package `{stats}`, which says: ::: {.mini} Multidimensional scaling takes a set of dissimilarities and returns a set of points such that the distances between the points are approximately equal to the dissimilarities. (It is a major part of what ecologists call ‘ordination’.) ::: I decided to connect the dots. I looked up its etymology, its history, and its relationship with other statistical terms. Then I realized, it is exactly the tool that can guide us through the ever-growing jungle of data.
